summary: Describes how http URIs can be fetched using TLS and HTTP/2 to blunt pervasive monitoring. It is not a replacement for https and is vulnerable to active attacks. This RFC is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: It puts a thin cover on web traffic so passive snoopers cannot read it. It is not as strong as the real lock, and it is no longer in use.

questions: what is opportunistic security for http
does opportunistic http/2 prevent man-in-the-middle attacks
subtitle: Light encryption for HTTP URIs using TLS and HTTP/2 to block passive eavesdropping.

tldr.problem: Many websites use plain HTTP, leaving traffic visible to passive monitors. Deploying HTTPS requires effort; some sites are reluctant or unable to migrate.
tldr.mechanism: The server advertises TLS+HTTP/2 as an alternative service for HTTP URIs. Clients can then fetch HTTP pages over an encrypted connection using HTTP/2, protecting against passive monitoring but not active attacks.
tldr.outcome: The specification was published as Experimental and is now Historic. Adoption was limited because HTTPS became easier to deploy and because this mechanism does not prevent man-in-the-middle attacks, making its security benefits unclear to users and operators.

today: RFC 8164 is Historic. The specification was published as Experimental in May 2017 but saw limited adoption. The rise of ACME and Let's Encrypt made HTTPS deployment easier, and because opportunistic security does not prevent active attacks, its practical benefits were unclear. Most modern browsers and servers focus on full HTTPS rather than opportunistic encryption for HTTP.

sections.title: Opportunistic Security: Protecting Against Passive Monitoring
sections.content:
Opportunistic Security is a approach that provides some protection most of the time, without the overhead and assurances of full authentication. RFC 8164 applies this concept to HTTP by allowing plain http URIs to be fetched over encrypted TLS+HTTP/2 connections.

The mechanism is intentionally simple: an origin server advertises an alternative service (HTTP/2 over TLS) for its HTTP URIs. Clients that support the specification can then route future HTTP requests for that origin through the TLS connection instead of plaintext, thereby defeating passive eavesdropping. This does not prevent active attacks (man-in-the-middle) and does not invoke HTTPS-level security policies, so users see no special security indicator.

The goal is to make HTTP more robust in the face of pervasive passive monitoring, while minimizing deployment friction.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of shouting your request across a crowded room, you whisper it through a tube. An eavesdropper in the room cannot hear, but someone inside the tube can still intercept it.

sections.title: How HTTP URIs Travel Over TLS
sections.content:
A server supporting this specification advertises alternative services using the Alt-Svc header field in HTTP responses. The advertisement points to a protocol identifier that uses TLS, such as h2 (HTTP/2). The HTTP/2 protocol is chosen because it includes an explicit :scheme field in requests, preventing confusion about whether the request is for http or https.

When a client receives the advertisement, it can store this information and use it for future requests to that origin. Before sending an HTTP request over the TLS connection, the client MUST verify that the server certificate is valid for the origin. The client MUST also obtain a valid http-opportunistic response from a well-known URI on the authenticated connection, confirming that the server has opted into serving HTTP over TLS.

This additional validation step prevents servers from accidentally or maliciously serving HTTP content over a TLS connection meant for HTTPS.
sections.plainLanguage: The server says "you can use the encrypted tunnel for your HTTP requests." The client checks that this is really the server it claims to be before trusting the tunnel.

sections.title: The http-opportunistic Well-Known URI
sections.content:
Clients validate alternative services using a well-known URI at /.well-known/http-opportunistic. The server must respond with a JSON array of origin strings. Each string is a case-insensitive match for origins that the server is willing to serve over the opportunistic encrypted connection.

The client caches the response if it is fresh and acquired over an authenticated connection. The cache must be cleared when other origin-based state (like cookies) is cleared, preventing long-term tracking. Cached responses obtained over an unauthenticated connection must not be used, as they cannot be trusted.

This mechanism ensures that servers explicitly opt in to serving HTTP over TLS, reducing the risk of confusion and misconfiguration.
sections.plainLanguage: The server publishes a signed list saying "these are the websites I will serve through the encrypted tunnel."

sections.title: Vulnerabilities and Limitations
sections.content:
The specification is vulnerable to active attacks (man-in-the-middle). Because there is no authentication guarantee, an attacker can intercept the Alt-Svc header field and remove or modify it, forcing the client back to plaintext. An attacker can also present a valid certificate (for a different site) and trick the client or server into treating the connection as authenticated when it should not be.

Implementations must not show security indicators (like a "lock" icon) that would suggest HTTPS-level trust. HTTP and HTTPS requests must not use the same connection, and HTTP requests for different origins must not share a connection, to prevent cross-site information leakage.

The mechanism is best suited for protecting against passive surveillance by ISPs and network operators, not against targeted attackers or compromised network infrastructure.
sections.plainLanguage: A bad actor on the network can cut the wire between you and the server, or pretend to be the server and intercept everything. This covers your tracks from passive snooping but not from active attacks.
